voiceover.text: So, why does more arousal help one athlete and wreck another? A powerlifter walks to the bar shouting, slapping their chest, breathing hard. Eight metres away, an archer is deliberately slowing their breathing until their heart rate drops. Both think they're doing the right thing. Write down what each is trying to achieve. Then the part that matters: are they chasing different goals, or the same goal from opposite starting points?

Arousal is your general level of activation. Its link with performance is an inverted U. Too little, and an athlete is flat: slow to react and not producing force. Too much, and performance falls again. Attention narrows so far that cues are missed, muscle tension disrupts coordination, decisions get rushed, and fine control breaks down. In between is the optimal arousal for that athlete and that task. And the optimum moves. As you saw with skill types in Year 11, a simple, forceful, gross task like a lift tolerates high arousal. A fine, precise task like archery or a putt needs it lower, because tension and narrow attention hurt it first. Experienced athletes often cope with more, and very anxious athletes usually need less. So the powerlifter and the archer want the same thing, their own optimum, from opposite sides. And one fired-up team talk can't suit everyone.

Stress is what happens when the demands of a situation are seen to exceed your resources. The word "seen" matters. Two players facing the same final-minute kick can feel very different stress, because they judge their resources differently. Eustress is the same arousal felt as excitement, not threat.

Anxiety is the unpleasant state stress can produce, and it has two halves. Cognitive anxiety is thinking: worry, doubt, attention on what might go wrong. Somatic anxiety is the body: a pounding heart, tense muscles, shaky breathing. They need different strategies. Give a worrier a breathing exercise, and their heart rate falls, but the worry keeps going. And the aim is never to remove anxiety completely. It's to manage it, and to read those body signals as readiness.

scenes.title: two thought strategies: goals and rehearsal

voiceover.text: Match each strategy to a problem, and say how it works. Goal setting helps with stress over results you can't control. Set process goals, like completing your routine on every shot, which you control even in a loss. An outcome goal like "win" adds stress, because the opponent has a say. Mental rehearsal means imagining a successful performance in detail. It builds confidence and fills attention with the task, so it suits cognitive anxiety.

Relaxation, slow breathing and progressive muscle relaxation, lowers somatic arousal directly. But use it on a flat athlete and you push them further below their optimum. Concentration strategies give attention a fixed target, like a cue word. Self-talk can be instructional, naming the key cue, or motivational, reframing nerves as readiness. And all of these are rehearsed in training, not invented in the final minute.

scenes.title: individual and group sports, and participation

voiceover.text: Individual and group sports create different pressures. An individual athlete carries the result alone, and nobody covers an error. In a team, pressure comes from teammates, selection and a role others rely on. A team room also holds many optimal levels at once, so it needs a shared framework plus individual routines, and teammates themselves become a resource that an individual athlete doesn't have. And half of this dot point is about participation, not just performance. Fear of being judged or of letting a team down is one of the main reasons young people stop playing. So strategies for participation look different: process goals that show improvement without winning, a mastery climate where effort and progress are praised, and a clear role for every player.

The verb is investigate, so evidence is part of the answer. Say what you claim, what evidence would support it, and what the evidence can't settle. The inverted U's broad shape is well supported, but a single precise optimum for each athlete is a simplification. Most evidence that a strategy works is self-report, athletes saying how anxious they felt, and people taught a strategy know what answer is expected. And in real sport, a strategy is rarely the only thing that changed.
Two things to remember. Optimal, not maximal. And treat the right half: body strategies for body signs, thought strategies for worry.

Two exam questions. First. A goalkicker who's accurate at training misses routine kicks in matches, with shaking hands and a pounding heart. A distance runner spends the two days before a race replaying a bad result and imagining being overtaken on the last lap. For each, name the problem, choose a strategy, and explain how it helps. Pause here to answer.

The goalkicker has somatic anxiety, so use relaxation, slow breathing built into the kicking routine, which lowers arousal toward the optimum for a precise skill. The runner has cognitive anxiety, so use mental rehearsal of a strong race and self-talk, which replace the failure images with the task. The classic mistake is giving both the same strategy.

Second. A team playing the bottom side is flat in the warm-up and concedes twice in ten minutes. And a fourteen-year-old is thinking of leaving the club, because they're afraid of making a mistake in front of teammates and being blamed. For each, identify the problem and recommend a strategy, explaining how it helps. Pause here to answer.

The team is under-aroused, so raise arousal, with an activation routine and process goals for the first ten minutes. The fourteen-year-old has a participation problem driven by fear of judgement, so build a mastery climate, with effort praised and a clear role. The classic mistake is treating the frightened player only as a performance problem.

So find each athlete's optimum for the task, work out which half of anxiety you're dealing with, match a rehearsed strategy to it, and judge the evidence honestly. That's the athlete's own mind. But on the day there's another side trying to stop you. What decides the strategies and tactics used on the day?
